submission.name: Quiet Quench
submission.tagline: A spoken nudge and splash for campus study sessions that keep getting interrupted.
submission.inspiration: We built this for students trying to study in busy dorms and shared apartments, where a phone break can turn into a long detour. We wanted a physical reminder that makes the interruption hard to ignore, with a voice that can call out the moment too.
submission.what_it_does: A webcam and YOLOv8 watch for a phone being picked up during a study session. When one appears, the app asks Gemini to check the image and come up with a short teasing line, then ElevenLabs reads it aloud while an Arduino switches on a small water pump.
submission.how_we_built_it: Python and OpenCV handle the webcam feed and YOLOv8 detection, while separate threads keep video capture moving during API requests. Gemini checks a detected phone and supplies the message; ElevenLabs turns that text into speech. An Arduino and relay control the pump when the laptop sends a trigger.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We planned to run the vision code on a Raspberry Pi, but the boards we had could not be brought up reliably. We moved the detection work to a laptop and used the Arduino for the pump, so the demo works but depends on the laptop staying connected and the camera seeing the desk.
submission.accomplishments: We got the camera detection, generated voice, and physical pump working together for a study-session demo. Adding a short pen tip to the outlet made the water stream more noticeable, and threading helped avoid freezing the camera while waiting for responses.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned how to wire a relay and microcontroller to a physical output, and how much time hardware setup can take. We also got practice with YOLOv8, concurrent tasks, and shaping text so a synthesized voice sounds like a quick interruption rather than a long announcement.
submission.whats_next: We would like to add a way to follow a student who moves away from the camera's view, and make the pump trigger safer to use around study materials. A more reliable single-board setup would also make it easier to move between desks.
